profiles.controversies: Compelled Emperor Theodosius I to perform public penance after the massacre at Thessalonica, and resisted the Empress Justina's attempt to grant a Milan church to Arian worship.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and Doctor of the Church, East and West
emphases: Vigorous defense of Nicene orthodoxy against Arianism in Milan
Assertion of the Church's independence from imperial authority
Liturgical hymnody and biblical commentary
profiles.name: Ambrose of Milan

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Ambrosius, St., bishop of Milan"

profiles.controversies: The author's true identity is unknown (the name 'Ambrosiaster' means 'pseudo-Ambrose,' since the work circulated for centuries under Ambrose's name); Hilary the deacon has been proposed as the author, on Augustine's testimony, but this remains disputed.
profiles.dates: 4th century (during the pontificate of Pope Damasus, 366–384)
emphases: Earliest complete Latin commentary on all the Pauline epistles
Commentary based on a pre-Vulgate Latin text of Paul
Engagement with contemporary 4th-century controversies (Arianism, Novatianism, Photinianism)
profiles.name: Ambrosiaster

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Ambrosiaster, or Pseudo-Ambrosius"

profiles.controversies: The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that modern scholarship restricts Ammonius's own contribution to what Eusebius describes of it (setting parallel Gospel passages beside Matthew's text), and now credits the numbered-section-and-canon-table cross-reference system itself to Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 265–340) rather than to Ammonius, even though the sections retained Ammonius's name in later manuscripts.
emphases: Composed a now-lost Harmony of the Gospels, arranging Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John's parallel passages together
The "Ammonian Sections" — the roughly 1,165-part division of the Gospels used for cross-reference in the manuscript tradition — carried his name for centuries
profiles.name: Ammonius of Alexandria

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907), s.v. "Ammonian Sections"

profiles.dates: active in the late 5th century (exact dates uncertain)
emphases: Author of the earliest surviving systematic Greek commentary on Revelation
Divided his commentary into 24 sections and 72 chapters, still used as a reference structure
Employed a threefold interpretive method (literal, moral, mystical)
profiles.name: Andreas of Caesarea
profiles.school: Byzantine — literal, moral and mystical exegesis

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Arethas, and Andreas"

emphases: 22 Demonstrations expounding Christian faith and practice for a Persian audience
Theology developed independently of the Greco-Roman doctrinal controversies of his time
Distinctive Semitic idiom, including feminine imagery for the Holy Spirit
profiles.name: Aphrahat the Persian Sage

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Aphraat (Aphrahat, Farhad)"

conciliarJudgment.note: The Second Ecumenical Council; also condemned at earlier Roman synods under Pope Damasus (377, 378).

profiles.controversies: Condemned at Rome under Pope Damasus (377, 378) and at the First Council of Constantinople (381), the Second Ecumenical Council, which held that an incomplete humanity in Christ could not secure the salvation of the whole human person.
emphases: Taught that the divine Logos took the place of a rational human mind in Christ, leaving Christ without a complete human nature
profiles.name: Apollinaris of Laodicea

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Apollinaris the Younger"

conciliarJudgment.note: The First Ecumenical Council; the Nicene Creed's homoousios clause was framed specifically against his teaching.

profiles.controversies: Condemned and excommunicated at the First Council of Nicaea (325), the First Ecumenical Council, which affirmed the Son as homoousios ('of one substance') with the Father specifically against his teaching.
emphases: Taught that the Son (the Logos) was a created being, not eternal or of one essence (homoousios) with the Father
Held there was 'a time when the Son was not'
profiles.name: Arius

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Arius"

profiles.controversies: Scholars have long debated whether the same author wrote both surviving works attributed to him, since they differ noticeably in their stance toward Augustinian teaching on grace.
emphases: Commentary on the Psalms
A dialogue work (the Altercatio) defending orthodox teaching against doctrinal error
profiles.name: Arnobius the Younger

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Arnobius, Junior"

profiles.controversies: Exiled five times over some seventeen years by Arian-sympathizing emperors for his defense of the Nicene Creed against Arius's teaching that the Son was a created being.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and Doctor of the Church, East and West
emphases: Full, eternal divinity of the Son against Arianism
'Of one substance' (homoousios) with the Father
The Incarnation as the ground of salvation
profiles.name: Athanasius of Alexandria

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Athanasius, St., archbishop of Alexandria"

profiles.controversies: Principal opponent of Donatism (a North African schism over the validity of sacraments administered by clergy who had lapsed under persecution) and of Pelagianism (denial that grace, rather than human effort, is necessary for salvation); his arguments shaped the West's rejection of both.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and Doctor of the Church, East and West
emphases: Divine grace as necessary for salvation, against Pelagius
Original sin and the bondage of the will
The City of God: a theology of history
profiles.name: Augustine of Hippo

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Augustinus, Aurelius"

profiles.controversies: Faced suspicion from some Western bishops and accusations of an unclear position on the Holy Spirit's divinity, and was pressured by the Arian-sympathizing Emperor Valens.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and Doctor of the Church, East and West; called 'the Great'
emphases: Defense of Nicene orthodoxy and the divinity of the Holy Spirit
Founder of Eastern coenobitic (communal) monastic rules
Practical charity — hospitals and poor-relief institutions
profiles.name: Basil of Caesarea
profiles.see: Bishop and Metropolitan of Caesarea in Cappadocia

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Basilius, called Basil the Great"

profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and Doctor of the Church (Roman Catholic, 1899); venerated 'the Venerable Bede'
emphases: Ecclesiastical History of the English People, the foundational source for early English Christianity
Extensive biblical commentaries synthesizing earlier patristic exegesis
Chronological and scientific writing (De Temporum Ratione)
profiles.name: Bede

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Beda, more correctly Baeda, The Venerable"

profiles.controversies: Took a moderating position in the grace/free-will debates that followed Augustine, opposing both strict double predestination and semi-Pelagian minimizing of grace.
emphases: Presided over the Second Council of Orange (529), which affirmed the necessity of grace against semi-Pelagianism while rejecting predestination to evil
Plain-spoken preaching against surviving pagan folk practice
Monastic rule-writing for women's communities
profiles.name: Caesarius of Arles
profiles.school: Western Latin theology (moderate Augustinian on grace)

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Caesarius (3), St., bishop of Arles"

emphases: Founded the monastery of Vivarium as a center of manuscript copying and Christian learning
Bridged classical Roman administration and monastic scholarship (having served as a minister to the Ostrogothic kings)
Institutiones — a guide to sacred and secular learning for monks
profiles.name: Cassiodorus

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Cassiodorus (or rather, Cassiodorius) Magnus Aurelius"

profiles.controversies: Some ancient and early-modern authorities questioned the full orthodoxy of specific speculative positions in his work, short of any formal condemnation.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Venerated as a saint in the early church; removed from the Roman Martyrology by Pope Clement VIII (later defended by Benedict XIV as a reasonable caution over some 'suspect' teaching, not a formal condemnation)
emphases: Head of the catechetical school of Alexandria; teacher of Origen
Synthesis of Greek philosophy with Christian faith (the Christian as true 'gnostic')
Protrepticus, Paedagogus and Stromateis — an ascending curriculum from conversion to mature faith
profiles.name: Clement of Alexandria

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Clement of Alexandria"

profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint, East and West; one of the Apostolic Fathers
emphases: First Epistle to the Corinthians — the earliest Christian document outside the New Testament to survive complete
Church order and the resolution of factional dispute
Apostolic succession of ministry
profiles.name: Clement of Rome

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Clemens Romanus"

profiles.controversies: The Catholic Encyclopedia states it is uncertain whether Cosmas was ever a Nestorian; "if it be necessary to suppose" that he was, it judges from his own Christian Topography that "at least towards the close of his life he returned to the orthodox faith." His flat-earth cosmological argument is described by the same source as "a curious attempt to harmonize a childish Biblical exegesis with ordinary phenomena" that "exercised no influence" on later thought.
profiles.dates: fl. first half of the 6th century
emphases: Wrote the Christian Topography (12 books), a literalist Biblical cosmology arguing against the spherical-earth astronomy of Ptolemy
Drew on firsthand experience as a former merchant who had sailed the Red Sea, Persian Gulf, and East African coast
profiles.name: Cosmas Indicopleustes
profiles.region: Alexandria, Egypt; extensive trading voyages on the Red Sea, Persian Gulf, and Indian Ocean; later the monastery of Raithu, Sinai

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia (1908), s.v. "Cosmas Indicopleustes"

profiles.controversies: Central to the 'lapsed' controversy (how to readmit Christians who had denied the faith under persecution) and the rebaptism controversy (whether baptism by schismatics or heretics was valid) — the latter placing him at odds with the Roman see.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and martyr, East and West
emphases: Episcopal authority as the foundation of church unity (De Unitate Ecclesiae)
Pastoral response to apostasy under persecution
Church discipline and order
profiles.name: Cyprian

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Cyprianus (1) Thascius Caecilius"

profiles.controversies: Led the condemnation of Nestorius at the Council of Ephesus (431); later reconciled with the Antiochene party under John of Antioch through a formula acknowledging two natures in the one Christ.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and Doctor of the Church, East and West
emphases: Theotokos ('God-bearer') as the correct title for Mary
The single, personal union of divine and human in Christ
Opposition to any teaching that divided Christ into two subjects
profiles.name: Cyril of Alexandria
profiles.school: Alexandrian — the personal (hypostatic) union of Christ's natures

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Cyrillus (7), St., archbishop of Alexandria"

profiles.controversies: Deposed three times in jurisdictional disputes with Acacius of Caesarea, before being restored under Theodosius I.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and Doctor of the Church, East and West
emphases: Catechetical Lectures — one of the earliest formal systems of Christian instruction
Mystagogical teaching on baptism and the Eucharist
Eventual acceptance of the Nicene homoousion at Constantinople (381)
profiles.name: Cyril of Jerusalem
profiles.school: Catechetical instruction, moving from semi-Arian sympathy toward Nicene orthodoxy

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Cyrillus (2), bishop of Jerusalem"

profiles.controversies: This entry represents an anonymous anthology, not a historical individual. The Catholic Encyclopedia's own account of its transmission cautions that, while the sayings are "in large measure authentic," "no doubt many were attributed to wrong persons, and many more were apocryphal inventions" — so an individual attribution within the collection (e.g., to "Abba So-and-so") should be treated as traditional rather than certain.
profiles.dates: Sayings originate among Egyptian hermits and monks of the 4th–5th centuries; collected and translated over subsequent centuries
emphases: A collection, not a person: aphorisms and anecdotes of Egyptian desert monks on ascetic and monastic life, gathered into alphabetical and topical Greek collections and Latin, Coptic, and Syriac versions
The Catholic Encyclopedia describes the material as combining "primitive freshness and quaintness" with real insight into human nature, alongside "a certain grotesque element"
profiles.language: Greek (collections also survive in Coptic, Latin, and Syriac)
profiles.name: Desert Fathers
profiles.region: The Egyptian desert (Scetis, Nitria, and the Cells)
profiles.school: Not a single author — an anonymous anthology of monastic sayings (the Apophthegmata Patrum, "Sayings of the Fathers"), not an individual church father

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907), s.v. "Apophthegmata"

profiles.controversies: His close intellectual dependence on Origen drew later suspicion during the Origenist controversies; some of his works were affected by the broader condemnation of Origenist teaching.
emphases: Head of the Alexandrian catechetical school, blind from early childhood
Extensive exegetical work, later translated into Latin by Jerome
Firm on the eternity of punishment, while entertaining Origenist speculation on other points
profiles.name: Didymus the Blind

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Didymus, head of catechetical school"

profiles.controversies: His Christological emphasis on Christ's distinct, complete humanity was later read by Cyril of Alexandria's party as a root of Nestorianism; some of his writings were included among the 'Three Chapters' controversy, though defenders such as Facundus of Hermiane argued for his orthodoxy.
emphases: Championed critical, historical and philological exegesis against allegory
Defended Nicene orthodoxy against Arianism at Antioch
Teacher of both John Chrysostom and Theodore of Mopsuestia
profiles.name: Diodorus of Tarsus
profiles.school: Antiochene — founder figure of the school's exegetical method

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Diodorus, presbyter of Antioch"

profiles.controversies: Was accused by some opponents in the Sabellian dispute of teaching a form of tritheism; Athanasius later examined the charge in detail and vindicated his orthodoxy.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Called 'the Great' by later tradition
emphases: Headed the Alexandrian catechetical school before his episcopate
Extensive correspondence addressing the 'lapsed' controversy and rebaptism dispute
Early engagement with the Sabellian controversy over the Trinity
profiles.name: Dionysius of Alexandria

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Dionysius of Alexandria"

profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint, East and West; Doctor of the Church (Roman Catholic, 1920)
emphases: Metrical hymns and verse homilies as a vehicle for doctrine
Scriptural exposition adopted widely into Syriac and other Eastern liturgies
Polemic against Gnostic and Marcionite teaching
profiles.name: Ephrem the Syrian

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Ephraim (4) the Syrian"

profiles.controversies: Held semi-Arian theological sympathies; subscribed to the Nicene Creed (325) with reservations about the term homoousios, and took part in synods that acted against Athanasius (Tyre, 335) and Marcellus of Ancyra.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Not canonized; read as the indispensable early church historian rather than venerated as a father in the full sense
emphases: Ecclesiastical History — the primary surviving narrative of Christianity from apostolic times to Constantine
Preservation of otherwise-lost early Christian sources and documents
Chronicle and apologetic works (Preparation for the Gospel, Proof of the Gospel)
profiles.name: Eusebius of Caesarea

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Eusebius of Caesarea"

profiles.controversies: His Origenist speculative theology (particularly on the pre-existence of souls) drew criticism from Jerome in his own lifetime, and later Origenist condemnations (6th century) affected the reception of his work, much of which survives only under other names or in Syriac translation.
emphases: Systematized the ascetic teaching of the Egyptian desert fathers
Influential doctrine of the eight evil thoughts (a source for the later 'seven deadly sins')
Teaching on apatheia (freedom from disordered passion) as the goal of the ascetic life
profiles.name: Evagrius Ponticus
profiles.region: Pontus; Constantinople; the Egyptian desert (Nitria, Scetis)

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Evagrius Ponticus, anchoret and writer"

profiles.controversies: Exiled twice to Sardinia during the persecution of Catholic bishops by the Arian Vandal king Thrasamund.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint, East and West
emphases: Closely followed Augustine on grace, predestination and the Trinity
Defended Chalcedonian orthodoxy against Arian Vandal rulers
Extensive theological correspondence and treatises written partly in exile
profiles.name: Fulgentius of Ruspe

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Fulgentius, Fabius Claudius Gordianus, bp. of Ruspe"

profiles.controversies: Withdrew from public teaching after Emperor Julian's 362 edict barring Christians from teaching classical literature.
emphases: Celebrated pagan rhetorician who converted to Christianity late in life
Wrote anti-Arian Trinitarian treatises and Pauline commentaries
Brought Neoplatonic philosophical vocabulary into Latin Christian theology
profiles.name: Gaius Marius Victorinus
profiles.school: Latin theology in dialogue with Neoplatonism

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Victorinus Afer"

profiles.controversies: Early polemical writings against Cyril of Alexandria (c. 431–432) drew criticism before the two were reconciled in 433.
emphases: Combated simony and enforced clerical discipline
Wrote a substantial commentary on Romans among other scriptural works
Opposed the Monophysite Timothy Aelurus's usurpation of the Alexandrian see
profiles.name: Gennadius of Constantinople

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Gennadius (10), bp. of Constantinople"

profiles.controversies: Resigned the see of Constantinople in the face of procedural objections to his election at the Council of Constantinople (381), despite having just helped secure the council's Nicene outcome.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and Doctor of the Church, East and West; called 'the Theologian' in Eastern Orthodoxy
emphases: Trinitarian theology delivered as oratory (the 'Five Theological Orations')
Restoration of Nicene faith at Constantinople
The full humanity of Christ as necessary for salvation
profiles.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
profiles.see: Bishop of Sasima; later Archbishop of Constantinople

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Gregorius Nazianzenus, bp. of Sasima and Constantinople"

profiles.controversies: Deposed by an Arian-dominated synod during the ascendancy of Emperor Valens and restored after Valens's death (378); some contemporaries suspected his Christology of tending toward positions later associated with Eutychianism.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint, East and West
emphases: Systematic Trinitarian and Christological theology
Mystical theology of the soul's ascent to God
Defense of orthodoxy against Arianism and Apollinarianism
profiles.name: Gregory of Nyssa

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Gregorius Nyssenus, bp. of Nyssa"

profiles.controversies: Strongly opposed the Patriarch of Constantinople's use of the title 'ecumenical bishop,' regarding it as a threat to the equal honor of the other patriarchates.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and Doctor of the Church, East and West
emphases: Consolidation of papal authority during the transition from Roman to medieval Western Christianity
Reform of monastic discipline and missionary expansion (the mission to England)
Pastoral and homiletic writing (Pastoral Rule, Moralia in Job)
profiles.name: Gregory the Dialogist
profiles.see: Bishop of Rome (Pope Gregory I, 'the Great')

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Gregorius I. (The Great), bp. of Rome"

profiles.controversies: A leading disciple of Valentinus; Clement of Alexandria called him the most esteemed of the Valentinian school, and Origen wrote an extensive refutation of his interpretations. No ecumenical council condemned him by name — he predates the conciliar era — but his teaching was never received by the wider church and was refuted at length by Irenaeus and Origen.
emphases: The earliest known commentator on the Gospel of John, of which around 50 quotations survive (chiefly preserved in Origen's own commentary, written to refute him)
Distinguished three fixed classes of humanity (material, psychic, spiritual) in his exegesis
profiles.name: Heracleon
profiles.region: Uncertain — possibly southern Italy, Sicily, or Alexandria

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Heracleon, a Gnostic"

profiles.controversies: Modern scholarship has had difficulty separating his authentic work from writings by other, later authors sharing his name.
emphases: Prolific commentator on both Testaments, ordained after a period as a desert monk
Homiletic and moral writing alongside scriptural commentary
profiles.name: Hesychius of Jerusalem

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Hesychius (25), presbyter of Jerusalem"

profiles.controversies: Came into sharp jurisdictional conflict with Pope Leo I (445) after deposing the bishop Chelidonius; Leo reversed the deposition and stripped Arles of its metropolitan authority, asserting Roman primacy over Gaul.
emphases: Monastic formation at Lérins before his episcopate
Vigorous, ascetic administration of the Gallic church
Regular episcopal visitation and synodal activity across Gaul
profiles.name: Hilary of Arles

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Hilarius Arelatensis, saint, bp. of Arles"

profiles.controversies: Exiled to Phrygia (356–360) by the Arian-sympathizing Emperor Constantius II for opposing Arian bishops.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and Doctor of the Church, East and West; called 'the Athanasius of the West'
emphases: De Trinitate — the first major Latin dogmatic treatment of the Trinity
One of the earliest Western Gospel commentaries (on Matthew)
Sustained opposition to Arianism in Gaul
profiles.name: Hilary of Poitiers

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Hilarius (7) Pictaviensis, saint"

profiles.controversies: Broke communion with Bishop Callistus of Rome over doctrinal and disciplinary disagreements and headed a separate community for a time; exiled to Sardinia c. 235, where he is said to have been reconciled to the wider church before his death.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and martyr, East and West
emphases: Extensive anti-heretical writing (Refutation of All Heresies)
Biblical commentary and chronography
Early witness to Roman liturgical and disciplinary practice
profiles.name: Hippolytus of Rome
profiles.see: Disputed — a rival bishop (or, per Roman tradition, presbyter) at Rome

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Hippolytus Romanus"

profiles.controversies: Scholars have long disputed which recension of his letters is genuine; the shorter ('middle') recension is generally accepted, and a longer recension is regarded as a later interpolation with Arian-era additions.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and martyr, East and West; one of the Apostolic Fathers
emphases: Seven letters written en route to martyrdom in Rome, key early evidence for episcopal church order
Eucharistic realism and the unity of the local church around its bishop
Opposition to docetic denial of Christ's real, physical incarnation
profiles.name: Ignatius of Antioch

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Ignatius, St., bp. of Antioch"

profiles.controversies: Engaged in the Quartodeciman controversy over the date of Easter, urging Rome toward leniency with Asian churches that differed from Roman practice.
emphases: Refutation of Valentinian Gnosticism in Against Heresies
Apostolic succession as the guarantee of true teaching
Recapitulation: Christ as the new Adam
profiles.language: Greek (works also survive in early Latin translation)
profiles.name: Irenaeus
profiles.region: Native of Asia Minor (Smyrna); Bishop of Lugdunum (Lyons), Gaul
profiles.school: Early Catholic — apostolic tradition and episcopal succession against Gnosticism

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Irenaeus, bp. of Lyons"

profiles.controversies: Formally a bishop of the Church of the East ("Nestorian" communion), consecrated by its Patriarch George. The Catholic Encyclopedia nonetheless observes that an extant prayer of his makes it "certainly difficult to realize that its author was a Nestorian," and separately records that Monophysite (Miaphysite) writers "falsified his biography" in an attempt to claim him for their own communion — so his own doctrinal self-identification is genuinely unsettled in the sources, not merely a labeling convenience.
profiles.dates: second half of the 7th century (consecrated bishop under Church of the East Patriarch George, 660–80); d. c. 700
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Venerated as a saint in the Eastern Orthodox and Eastern Catholic Churches, notwithstanding his formal Church of the East communion — see Controversies
emphases: Resigned his episcopate after only five months, for reasons the sources do not record, and retired to monastic solitude
His Ascetical Homilies were, per the Catholic Encyclopedia, "for centuries the main food of Syrian piety" and were translated into Arabic, Ethiopic, and Greek
profiles.name: Isaac of Nineveh
profiles.region: Nineveh; later the monastery of Rabban Shapur, Khuzistan (Persia)
profiles.school: Church of the East ("Nestorian" communion) — ascetical and mystical theology
profiles.see: Bishop of Nineveh (resigned the see after five months)

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), s.v. "Isaac of Nineveh"

profiles.controversies: Disputed sharply with his former friend Rufinus over the orthodoxy of Origen's teaching and Rufinus's translation of Origen's On First Principles; also opposed Pelagius's teaching on grace and free will.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and Doctor of the Church, East and West
emphases: Translation of the Old Testament from Hebrew and the New Testament from Greek into Latin (the Vulgate)
Biblical scholarship grounded in the original languages
Ascetic and monastic writings
profiles.name: Jerome

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Hieronymus, Eusebius (Jerome), saint"

profiles.controversies: His writings on grace and free will were criticized by Augustine's disciple Prosper of Aquitaine as insufficiently clear on the priority of grace — the position later labelled 'semi-Pelagian.'
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Venerated as a saint in Eastern Orthodoxy and in Gallic tradition; not formally canonized in the wider Roman calendar
emphases: 'Founder of Western monasticism' — brought Egyptian monastic practice to Gaul (Institutes, Conferences)
A middle position between Pelagianism and strict Augustinian predestination
Practical spiritual direction for ascetic communities
profiles.name: John Cassian
profiles.region: Egypt and Constantinople; later Marseilles, Gaul
profiles.school: Latin monastic theology, transmitting Eastern practice westward

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Cassianus (11) Johannes"

profiles.controversies: Deposed in 403 by the 'Synod of the Oak' through the influence of the Empress Eudoxia and Patriarch Theophilus of Alexandria; briefly restored, then permanently exiled and died in exile at Pityus.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and Doctor of the Church, East and West; one of the Three Holy Hierarchs in Eastern Orthodoxy
emphases: Grammatical-historical (not allegorical) exposition of Scripture
Extensive verse-by-verse homilies on both Testaments
Pastoral and moral application of the text
profiles.name: John Chrysostom

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Chrysostom, John"

profiles.controversies: Wrote from outside the Byzantine Empire (under Umayyad rule) in defense of icon veneration against the iconoclast policy of Emperor Leo III.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and Doctor of the Church, East and West; traditionally reckoned the last of the Greek Fathers
emphases: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith — the earliest systematic summary of Greek patristic doctrine
Defense of the veneration of icons during the Iconoclast Controversy
Synthesis, rather than innovation, of earlier patristic teaching
profiles.name: John Damascene
profiles.region: Damascus; later the monastery of Mar Saba near Jerusalem

sources.title: Philip Schaff (ed.), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 9 (Hilary of Poitiers, John of Damascus) — CCEL

conciliarJudgment.note: The Third Ecumenical Council named him explicitly in confirming Pelagianism's condemnation; he had already been deposed by imperial edict in 418 and condemned again at Rome in 430.

profiles.controversies: Deposed and exiled by imperial edict (418) for refusing to subscribe to Pope Zosimus's condemnation of Pelagianism; condemned again at a Roman council under Pope Celestine I (430) and explicitly named at the Council of Ephesus (431), the Third Ecumenical Council.
emphases: The most articulate theological defender of Pelagian teaching against Augustine after Pelagius's own condemnation
Extensive polemical exchange directly with Augustine on grace, original sin and concupiscence
profiles.name: Julian of Eclanum
profiles.school: Leading defender of Pelagianism after Pelagius

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Julianus Eclanensis, bp. of Eclana"

profiles.controversies: Martyred at Rome, traditionally after conflict with the Cynic philosopher Crescens.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and martyr, East and West
emphases: Philosophical defense of Christianity to Roman emperors (the Apologies)
Dialogue with Trypho — early Christian engagement with Judaism
Christ as the pre-existent divine Logos
profiles.name: Justin Martyr
profiles.region: Born at Flavia Neapolis, Palestine; taught and died at Rome

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Justinus Martyr, philosopher"

profiles.controversies: His legates' Tome was received as authoritative at the Council of Chalcedon (451), but Leo himself rejected the council's Canon 28 elevating Constantinople's ecclesiastical rank, a dispute that was never fully resolved in his lifetime.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and Doctor of the Church, East and West
emphases: The Tome of Leo (449), a defining statement of two-natures Christology adopted at Chalcedon
Assertion of the primacy of the Roman see over other patriarchates
Vigorous action against Manichaeans, Pelagians and Priscillianists in Italy
profiles.name: Leo the Great

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Leo I., the Great"

profiles.controversies: Some scholars have debated whether his Trinitarian language shows subordinationist tendencies, though the surviving text gives no clear evidence of the error.
emphases: Celebrated for elegant Ciceronian Latin prose — called 'the Christian Cicero'
Divine Institutes, a systematic apologetic defense of Christianity against pagan philosophy
Tutor to Crispus, son of the Emperor Constantine
profiles.name: Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius
profiles.region: Roman North Africa; later Nicomedia and Gaul

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Lactantius"

profiles.controversies: Wace & Piercy's Dictionary notes that a number of works transmitted under Maximus's name were in fact wrongly attributed to him and belong to Augustine, Ambrose, or Leo the Great, and that two treatises circulating under his name (Contra Paganos and Contra Judaeos) are "of very doubtful authority."
profiles.dates: 5th century (documented at councils in 451 and 465); Gennadius's claim that he died before 423 is contradicted by internal evidence in his own homilies
emphases: Left 117 homilies and 116 sermons, chiefly on liturgical practice, feast-day observance, and church discipline
Homilies document contemporary events, including local pagan superstitions and the effects of Attila's invasion of northern Italy in 452
On the relative authority of Peter and Paul, called Peter "the keystone of the church" while also allowing that "who should be preferred to whom remains uncertain"
profiles.name: Maximus of Turin

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Maximus, bp. of Turin"

profiles.controversies: A leading early opponent of Origen's theology, particularly its view of the resurrection body.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and martyr in Eastern Orthodoxy
emphases: The Symposium (Banquet of the Ten Virgins), modeled on Plato, in praise of virginity
Systematic refutation of Origen's teaching on the resurrection and the eternity of the world
Affirmed the full divinity of Christ
profiles.name: Methodius of Olympus
profiles.school: Asia Minor — Platonic dialogue form, anti-Origenist
profiles.see: Bishop of Olympus, later of Patara

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Methodius"

conciliarJudgment.note: A local Roman synod, not an ecumenical council; excommunicated for schism over the treatment of the lapsed, not for a Trinitarian heresy.

profiles.controversies: Formally excommunicated by a synod of 60 bishops at Rome in late 251 after setting himself up as a rival bishop against Cornelius; he organized a separate, schismatic church that persisted for centuries.
emphases: Orthodox on Trinitarian doctrine; wrote an early Latin treatise De Trinitate
Rigorist position that the church could not readmit Christians who had lapsed under persecution
profiles.name: Novatian
profiles.school: Rigorist schism (theology otherwise largely orthodox on the Trinity)

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Novatianus and Novatianism"

profiles.controversies: This is one name covering more than one authorship problem, not a single settled author. The Catholic Encyclopedia calls the question 'a riddle that can be solved only by thorough critical study of the manuscripts in connexion with the whole question of the Catenae': the Apocalypse commentary reworks Andrew of Caesarea; the Acts/Catholic Epistles commentaries duplicate Theophylact of Ohrid's (an 11th-century writer, even though the Oecumenius manuscripts are earlier); the Pauline commentary is a separate, still different work; and 'Oecumenius' is himself cited as a source inside these very commentaries. This app's own database labels part of the Hebrews material 'The Pseudo-Oecumenian Catena on Hebrews,' acknowledging the same problem. Readers should treat 'Oecumenius' as a traditional label for a body of Byzantine catena material of composite and, in places, pseudonymous origin, not as one person's original commentary.
profiles.dates: Traditionally dated c. 990 as Bishop of Trikka, based on a 10th/11th-century manuscript attribution; the Catholic Encyclopedia treats this dating and even the underlying authorship as unresolved (see Controversies).
emphases: Commentaries transmitted under this name cover Acts, the Pauline and Catholic Epistles, and Revelation
The Apocalypse commentary is, per the Catholic Encyclopedia, 'a slightly modified version of the commentary of Andrew of Caesarea' (6th century)
The Acts and Catholic Epistles commentaries are textually identical to the 11th-century Theophylact of Ohrid's, despite manuscripts under Oecumenius's name predating him
profiles.name: Oecumenius
profiles.school: Byzantine catena tradition — compiled, derivative exegesis rather than a single original voice
profiles.see: Bishop of Trikka (traditional attribution; authorship of the works themselves is disputed)

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), s.v. "Œcumenius, Bishop of Trikka"

profiles.controversies: Excommunicated by his own bishop, Demetrius of Alexandria, c. 231 over disciplinary irregularities in his ordination and doctrinal disagreement — a judgment other churches did not uniformly accept. Centuries later, a set of propositions associated with 'Origenism' (not proven to be Origen's own words in every case) were anathematized by a synod under Justinian (543) and are traditionally, though disputedly, linked to the Fifth Ecumenical Council (Second Council of Constantinople, 553); historians differ on whether the council's authentic acts condemned Origen by name or only later 6th-century Origenist teaching. Throughline lists him in the default bank, labelled with this nuance rather than treated as a condemned heresiarch.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Universally counted a foundational patristic scholar; never canonized, and specific propositions attributed to his followers were later anathematized (see below)
emphases: Head of the Alexandrian catechetical school from age 18; pioneer of systematic Christian theology (De Principiis)
Comprehensive, verse-by-verse biblical commentary at a scale no predecessor had attempted
The Hexapla — a six-column comparative edition of the Old Testament text
profiles.name: Origen of Alexandria
profiles.region: Alexandria; later Caesarea in Palestine (from c. 231)

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Origenes, known as Origen"

profiles.controversies: His surviving writings chiefly oppose Novatianism, a rigorist schism that denied the church's power to readmit the lapsed to communion. Jerome records that Pacian died at an advanced age under the emperor Theodosius.
profiles.dates: Bishop from c. 365; died in extreme old age during the reign of Theodosius (d. c. 391)
emphases: Jerome's Lives of Illustrious Men calls him "a man of chaste eloquence, and as distinguished by his life as by his speech"
Wrote against the Novatianists, including a treatise nicknamed The Deer (Cervus) and another Against the Novatians
profiles.name: Pacian of Barcelona
profiles.school: Western Latin — anti-Novatianist polemic and pastoral instruction

sources.title: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, "Pacianus the Bishop," in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 3 (ed. Philip Schaff)

conciliarJudgment.note: The Third Ecumenical Council confirmed Pelagianism's condemnation, which earlier North African synods (Carthage, 411–418) had already pronounced.

profiles.controversies: Condemned at synods of Carthage (411, 416, and again by 214 bishops on 1 May 418) and definitively at the Council of Ephesus (431), the Third Ecumenical Council, which confirmed Pelagianism's condemnation alongside its ruling against Nestorius. Augustine's writings against him were decisive for the West's rejection of his teaching.
emphases: Taught that human beings could, by will and effort, achieve moral perfection and merit salvation without a decisive prior act of divine grace
Denied that Adam's sin is transmitted to his descendants as guilt
profiles.name: Pelagius
profiles.region: Traditionally British; taught chiefly at Rome, then North Africa and the East

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Pelagianism and Pelagius"

profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and Doctor of the Church, East and West
emphases: 176 short, clear surviving sermons focused on Gospel parables and miracles
Preaching praised for clarity over literary ornament ('Chrysologus,' 'of the golden word')
Most of his other writings were lost to later fires at Ravenna
profiles.name: Peter Chrysologus

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Chrysologus, Petrus"

profiles.controversies: A leading opponent of the Council of Chalcedon's dyophysite Christology. Installed as bishop in 485 with the backing of the Miaphysite patriarch Peter the Fuller, he campaigned against the Chalcedonian patriarch Flavian of Antioch and secured his deposition at the Synod of Sidon (512). When the pro-Chalcedonian emperor Justin I came to power in 518, Philoxenus was banished, first to Thrace and then to Gangra in Paphlagonia, where the Dictionary of Christian Biography records that he died "of suffocation by smoke."
emphases: With Severus of Antioch, formulated Jacobite Miaphysite Christology ("one nature composed of two") against Chalcedon
Held a Theopaschite position: that God the Word himself, and not only the man Christ, suffered
Commissioned his chorepiscopus Polycarp to produce the Philoxenian Syriac version of the New Testament (508), an extremely literal translation later revised by Thomas of Harkel
profiles.name: Philoxenus of Mabbug
profiles.region: Born in Tahal, Beth Garmai (near modern Kirkuk); bishop at Hierapolis (Mabbug), Syria; died in exile at Gangra, Paphlagonia
profiles.school: Syriac Miaphysite ("Monophysite") — one united nature of Christ, opposed to the Council of Chalcedon's two-nature definition

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Philoxenus, a Monophysite leader"

profiles.controversies: Central figure in the Quartodeciman dispute over the date of Easter, maintaining the Asian tradition against Rome's practice.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Saint and martyr, East and West; one of the Apostolic Fathers
emphases: Epistle to the Philippians, an early witness to apostolic teaching
Opposition to Gnostic and Marcionite doctrine
Martyrdom account (Martyrdom of Polycarp) as an early model of Christian witness under persecution
profiles.name: Polycarp of Smyrna

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Polycarpus, bishop of Smyrna"

profiles.controversies: Wace & Piercy's Dictionary records that Primasius at first opposed condemning the "Three Chapters" and signed Pope Vigilius's Constitutum against their condemnation (553), but later reversed himself and signed the Council's own decrees once Vigilius did — a reversal the Dictionary connects to his ambition to succeed the primate of Byzacena after that primate's death.
emphases: Wrote commentaries on the Pauline Epistles and on the Apocalypse
Drawn into the Three Chapters controversy as one of the North African bishops summoned to Constantinople in the events leading to the Fifth Ecumenical Council (553)
profiles.name: Primasius of Hadrumetum
profiles.region: Hadrumetum (Justinianopolis), Byzacena, Roman North Africa (modern Tunisia)
profiles.school: Western Latin (North African) — commentary on the Pauline Epistles and the Apocalypse

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Primasius, bp. of Adrumetum"

profiles.dates: c. 465 – c. 530 (active under the emperors Justin and Justinian)
emphases: A Christian sophist and rhetorician who taught the sophist Choricius of Gaza
His scripture commentaries — catena-style works on the Octateuch and on Isaiah — are, per Wace's Dictionary, abridgements of larger collections of earlier interpreters that he had compiled himself
Wace's Dictionary describes his stated positions on the Trinity and on the authority of Scripture as doctrinally unexceptionable ("satisfactory")
profiles.name: Procopius of Gaza
profiles.school: Rhetorical School of Gaza — catena-style biblical exegesis

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Procopius Gazaeus, a Christian sophist" (CCEL)

profiles.controversies: The Catholic Encyclopedia states that orthodoxy dominates his work and that he attacked the ancient heresies, though he engages contemporary Arianism only lightly and follows Tertullian closely; it also notes his doctrinal statements "occasionally contained errors" despite his considerable learning.
emphases: A former lawyer and provincial governor who turned to writing Christian poetry late in life, after imperial court service

The Cathemerinon (hymns for the hours of the day) and the allegorical Psychomachia ("Battle of the Soul") — per the Catholic Encyclopedia, "the model of a style destined to be lovingly cultivated in the Middle Ages"
Also wrote the Peristephanon (poems on the martyrs), the doctrinal Apotheosis and Hamartigenia, and the apologetic Contra Symmachum
profiles.name: Prudentius
profiles.region: Tarraconensis, Roman Spain; died in Spain

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), s.v. "Aurelius Clemens Prudentius"

profiles.controversies: Not a church father: a Carolingian scholar who died in 908. His Gospel comments reach readers mainly through Thomas Aquinas's 13th-century Catena Aurea, which cites him simply as "Remigius". The source database files this material under Remigius of Rheims (d. c. 533), the "Apostle of the Franks", whose surviving work Wace & Piercy (1911) list as four letters, a spurious will and a few verses — no biblical commentary. The attribution is corrected here; the material is kept, clearly dated, because it is widely quoted in the catena tradition.
profiles.dates: born about the middle of the 9th century; died 908 — Carolingian, after this app's c. AD 800 patristic cutoff
emphases: Benedictine monk of St-Germain, Auxerre; taught at Auxerre, Paris and Reims (pupil of Heiric of Auxerre and Dunchad of Reims)
Wrote glosses and marginal commentaries on the Bible and an exposition of the Psalms, alongside commentaries on Priscian, Boethius's Opuscula Sacra and Martianus Capella
On universals, sought a middle way between Eriugena's realism and the anti-realism of his teacher Heiric
profiles.name: Remigius of Auxerre
profiles.school: Carolingian school of Auxerre — grammarian and glossator; post-patristic

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Remigius, St., archbp. of Rheims"
Catholic Encyclopedia (1911), s.v. "Remigius of Auxerre"

profiles.dates: c. 400 – after 480 (Gennadius, writing c. 490s, describes him as by then of "a good old age")
emphases: Gennadius calls him "a master among bishops," learned in secular and sacred literature, who wrote in a clear, scholastic style
His chief surviving work, several books On the Governance of God (De Gubernatione Dei), reads contemporary disasters and the barbarian invasions as divine providence responding to Roman moral failure
Also wrote books on virginity, against avarice, a commentary on Ecclesiastes, and a collection of letters
profiles.name: Salvian the Presbyter
profiles.region: Native of the Trier region; presbyter at Marseilles (Massilia), Gaul
profiles.school: Western Latin (Gallic) — moral and providential historiography

sources.title: Gennadius of Marseilles, Lives of Illustrious Men, "Salvianus the Presbyter," in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 3 (ed. Philip Schaff)

profiles.controversies: Initially welcomed to Constantinople by John Chrysostom, who gave him pulpit prominence and, during his own absence in 401, deputed him real administrative authority. Severian turned against his patron, cultivated the alienated clergy and the imperial court, and joined the party that condemned Chrysostom at the Synod of the Oak (403). Wace & Piercy's Dictionary records that Severian later used his influence to have the exiled Chrysostom moved from the comparatively mild Cucusus to the harsher outpost of Pityus.
emphases: Praised by his contemporary Gennadius as "learned in the Scriptures and an admirable preacher"
Numerous homilies on subjects including Creation and the Nativity survive complete or as catena fragments on the Pauline Epistles and Hebrews
profiles.name: Severian of Gabala
profiles.region: Gabala, coastal Syria; later active at Constantinople

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Severianus, bp. of Gabala"

profiles.controversies: After Justin Martyr's death he adopted rigorist 'Encratite' asceticism (rejecting marriage and meat), which Irenaeus and later writers judged heretical. No council condemned him by name — a formal conciliar mechanism did not yet exist in his lifetime — the church's judgment against him rests on the Fathers' own writings (chiefly Irenaeus), not a synodal act.
emphases: Compiled the Diatessaron, an influential early harmony of the four Gospels
Address to the Greeks, an apologetic work while still associated with Justin Martyr
profiles.name: Tatian the Assyrian
profiles.region: Born east of the Tigris (Assyria); taught at Rome; later Mesopotamia/Edessa

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Tatianus"

profiles.controversies: In later life adopted the rigorist Montanist movement and its stricter asceticism, and wrote increasingly bitter polemic against the mainstream church's clergy — after which his later work is read as that of a separated Montanist, not a communicant of the wider church.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Never canonized (his later Montanism is the traditional reason); nonetheless universally read as a foundational Latin theological voice
emphases: Coined much of the Latin theological vocabulary later councils relied on (trinitas, persona, substantia)
Vigorous apologetic defense of Christianity against pagan critics
Early formulations bearing on Trinitarian and Christological doctrine
profiles.name: Tertullian
profiles.school: Latin North African — first major Latin theological writer

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Tertullianus, Quintus Septimius Florens"

conciliarJudgment.note: The Fifth Ecumenical Council; posthumous condemnation as part of the 'Three Chapters' controversy. He was not condemned in his own lifetime and died in communion with the church.

profiles.controversies: Died 'in the peace of the church,' but was condemned posthumously, together with certain writings of Theodoret of Cyrus and a letter of Ibas of Edessa (the 'Three Chapters'), at the Second Council of Constantinople in 553 — the Fifth Ecumenical Council — for Christological teaching later read as a root of Nestorianism.
emphases: Prominent biblical commentator in the Antiochene grammatical-historical tradition
Emphasized the full, complete humanity of Christ
Died in full communion with the church, well regarded in his own lifetime
profiles.name: Theodore of Mopsuestia

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Theodorus, bp. of Mopsuestia"

profiles.controversies: A student of Theodore of Mopsuestia, he initially resisted Cyril of Alexandria's anathemas against Nestorius; condemned at the 'Robber Synod' of Ephesus (449), then restored to his see at the Council of Chalcedon (451) after formally anathematizing Nestorius. His anti-Cyril writings were among the 'Three Chapters' condemned at the Second Council of Constantinople (553) — his person was not condemned, only those specific writings.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Venerated as a saint in some Eastern traditions; his standing was long contested in the West over the Three Chapters
emphases: Extensive biblical commentary in the Antiochene literal-historical tradition
Ecclesiastical History continuing Eusebius's narrative
Compendium of Heretical Fables, a survey of doctrinal error
profiles.name: Theodoret of Cyrus

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Theodoretus, bishop of Cyrrhus"

profiles.controversies: A member of the Donatist schism (which held that sacraments administered by clergy who had lapsed under persecution were invalid), though he broke with the Donatist mainstream over the question of whether the true church could be a small remnant rather than a worldwide body — a moderation Augustine engaged with directly.
emphases: The Book of Rules, the first Latin treatise on principles of biblical interpretation
Widely used by Augustine and later Latin exegetes despite the author's own schismatic affiliation
Distinctive reading of Revelation later influential on Western apocalyptic commentary
profiles.name: Ticonius

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Tichonius, an African Donatist"

profiles.controversies: The Emperor Julian sought to have him expelled from Bostra in 362 on a disputed charge of inciting unrest against the city's pagan population.
emphases: Four-book refutation of Manichaeism, praised by Jerome
Cited and preserved in part by Epiphanius and Theodoret
profiles.name: Titus of Bostra

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Titus, bishop of Bostra"

profiles.controversies: Engaged in a bitter public dispute with his former friend Jerome over his translation of Origen's On First Principles, which Jerome accused of softening Origen's heterodox passages.
emphases: Translated Origen, Eusebius and other Greek fathers into Latin, opening their work to Western readers
Own Church History continuing Eusebius
Commentary on the Apostles' Creed
profiles.name: Tyrannius Rufinus

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Rufinus of Aquileia"

profiles.controversies: His system became the primary target of Irenaeus's Against Heresies (c. 180–185) and was also opposed by Tertullian and Justin Martyr. No ecumenical council condemned him by name — he predates the conciliar era — but the wider church rejected his teaching as heretical from an early date, well attested in the Fathers' own writings.
emphases: Systematized an elaborate Gnostic cosmology of divine emanations ('Aeons')
Initially regarded as orthodox at Alexandria and Rome before his teaching was rejected
profiles.name: Valentinus

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Valentinus, founder of a Gnostic sect"

profiles.controversies: His millenarianism (belief in a literal future earthly reign of Christ) was outside the mainstream even in his own period, and little of his authentic work survives unedited.
profiles.ecclesialRecognition: Venerated as a martyr; his millenarian views led some later works attributed to him to be classed as apocryphal
emphases: Among the earliest Latin biblical commentators
Commentary on Revelation, notable for its millenarian (chiliastic) reading
Jerome records that he drew heavily on Origen despite writing in Latin
profiles.language: Greek by birth; wrote in Latin
profiles.name: Victorinus of Pettau

sources.title: Wace & Piercy, A Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature to the End of the Sixth Century (1911), s.v. "Victorinus"
